hypotheses.statement: The proximal trigger of the alopecia areata T-cell attack is collapse of hair-follicle immune privilege, via IFN-γ-driven MHC class I upregulation on follicular epithelium and CXCL9/CXCL10-mediated recruitment of CD8+ NKG2D+ cytotoxic T cells.

IL-15 signaling contributes at the trigger/amplifier level to the alopecia areata T-cell attack by driving loss of immune tolerance and activation/expansion of CD8+ NKG2D+ effector T cells against hair-follicle antigens.

Age- and phenotype-specific clustering of atopic and autoimmune comorbidities in alopecia areata patients suggests either shared upstream immune-dysregulation pathways or distinct AA endotypes that lower the threshold for the follicular T-cell attack, rather than a single uniform trigger.
Inherited variation at HLA class II and NKG2D-ligand loci lowers the threshold for the alopecia areata T-cell attack, functioning as susceptibility architecture rather than the acute trigger itself.

The alopecia areata T-cell attack results from a multi-hit threshold process in which inherited immune-susceptibility variants combine with a second, currently unspecified exogenous or endogenous hit to collapse hair-follicle immune privilege past a critical threshold.
Exogenous exposures such as psychological stress or infection may act as a second hit that precipitates the alopecia areata T-cell attack in genetically predisposed individuals.

γc-cytokine/JAK-STAT signaling is a common downstream effector pathway through which the alopecia areata T-cell attack is executed, though this is currently better supported as a treatment-response observation than as evidence of an initiating cause.
